fields.question: Why add a visual-need router after building caption memory?
fields.answer: Text remembers broad events but may omit details needed later. The router decides whether text evidence suffices and spends more vision budget only when needed. This controls evidence-acquisition cost; captions are not lossless and a routing decision is not an answer.
fields.example: “Someone picks up a box” can answer whether an object was taken, but reading its serial number may require looking at frames.

fields.question: Does caption-once mean writing a new video caption for each question?
fields.answer: No. Build one reusable text memory, then route and budget additional vision separately for each question. Count initial captioning and per-query frame access separately; memory reuse does not mean all queries avoid visual compute.
fields.example: Five questions can share one caption, and only the question needing additional detail may require frames.

fields.question: What is the trade-off versus uniformly resampling the video for every question?
fields.answer: Uniform sampling repeatedly pays vision cost. On-demand access reuses a caption and focuses on uncertain frames, but a missed detail or routing error can hide key evidence. Compare real quality on identical questions and budgets.
fields.example: Ten event-order queries may share memory; a brief action in the last query still needs the right frame.

fields.question: Do three-seed local caption/query gates validate the learned visual-need router?
fields.answer: No. Reference state transitions check gating, top-K frame selection, and budget; there is no long-video VLM or trained semantic router. This does not prove the system can tell which questions text answers or reproduce frame savings.
fields.example: A rule can select at most three frames without knowing whether any contains the answer.

fields.question: Why train the HAWK drafter on shifted trajectories after its own proposals?
fields.answer: Proposed tokens put the system on drafter-generated prefixes. Training only on teacher prefixes hides that shift. Shifted trajectories align supervision with actual proposal states, and a mix of teacher layers conveys visual information. The target must still verify acceptance.
fields.example: If the first draft token chooses different wording, the second should learn the target distribution under that actual prefix.

fields.question: What are the target and drafter roles in HAWK speculative decoding?
fields.answer: The cheaper drafter proposes tokens; the target verifies them and preserves the output distribution. HAWK compresses multiple target layers for a shallow drafter to improve proposals, not to bypass verification.
fields.example: A shallow model proposes several words, then the larger model checks how many can be accepted.

fields.question: How does HAWK's learned layer mix differ from using only the final target layer?
fields.answer: Softmax-normalized trainable weights combine hidden states from multiple layers; final-only is a fixed choice of one source. Weights sum to one but need not be equal. Mixing alone proves neither acceptance-rate gains nor speed.
fields.example: A high layer weight increases its share in the mixed representation rather than concatenating layers as extra tokens.

fields.question: Does local HAWK validation include a specialized decoding kernel?
fields.answer: No. It checks softmax-weighted target hidden states, shifted-target supervision, and target isolation. It does not run a complete speculative verification loop or specialized kernel, so cannot demonstrate end-to-end lossless speedup.
fields.example: Checking that three weights sum to one does not measure accepted tokens or saved generation time.

fields.question: Why is three local layers followed by one global layer different from shortening every context window?
fields.answer: Local layers limit most interactions, while global layers still exchange distant information. GQA separately reduces KV heads. These are architectural trade-offs, not reproduction of distillation, post-training, or device performance.
fields.example: A distant heading can affect the current paragraph in a global layer, while local layers process adjacent sentences.

fields.question: Why count weights, KV, vision, and drafter memory together for Muse Glimmer?
fields.answer: Device memory must hold the entire inference process. Long agent context grows KV, and vision and speculative heads add memory. A quantized language model under a size cap does not alone fit a 32GB device. Use real inputs and deployment settings.
fields.example: Weights below 20 GB may still leave too little space for long-trajectory KV and temporary vision tensors.

fields.question: How does late-stage cross-entropy differ from fitting truncated teacher logits?
fields.answer: Distillation uses teacher predictions, but top-k truncation drops the tail. Late cross-entropy directly supervises the target token; the paper connects the switch to truncation bias. It is not correct to describe the entire recipe as teacher matching.
fields.example: CE still uses a target token even if the saved teacher top-k omitted it.

fields.question: Can the 52 layers share one attention and RoPE template?
fields.answer: No. Repeat [Local, Local, Local, Global] 13 times with 32 query heads and two KV heads. Only local layers apply RoPE. The vision branch separately compresses 1024 patches to 256 tokens via 2×2 grouping. One layer is not the 29.6B model.
fields.example: Applying RoPE everywhere or alternating local and global changes the architecture even with 52 layers.

fields.question: Why re-estimate FFN channel importance after pruning attention paths?
fields.answer: Pruning changes FFN input distributions, making old rankings stale. MWOP treats paths such as vision→vision and text→vision separately and prunes FFN channels by modality. Measure quality and actual speed independently.
fields.example: Removing text-to-vision paths can change how much fusion channels contribute.

fields.question: Why can one MWOP attention head have different modality-path importance?
fields.answer: One head can support vision→vision, text→vision, and text→text interactions with unequal contributions. MWOP assesses and prunes paths within a head rather than treating it as indivisible.
fields.example: Keep text reading vision in a head that contributes little to vision-only interaction.

fields.question: What changes with modality-specific FFN pruning instead of one common channel mask?
fields.answer: Text and vision tokens can retain different channel sets and capacities. One mask may hide different channel contributions. Sparse masking needs execution support; it does not guarantee hardware speedup.
fields.example: Text-related channels and texture channels may not overlap. Separate masks preserve both kinds, but the kernel must actually skip work.

fields.question: Why not rank MWOP pruning by |w| rather than |w·∂L/∂w|?
fields.answer: The product captures magnitude and current loss sensitivity. Magnitude alone omits sensitivity; absolute value prevents signed contributions from canceling. This local estimate depends on calibration data and path, not a guarantee deletion is harmless.
fields.example: Two equal weights with different gradients rank differently under the product but tie by magnitude.

fields.question: Why not share one global quantization range and rotation across multimodal KV?
fields.answer: Keys may drift over time so a global range loses local precision. Value geometry also differs by modality. Short-window ranges handle temporal shifts and modality-specific rotations handle value geometry; one static rule need not control both errors.
fields.example: Small audio keys can lose precision when later video keys set the global range; value structure still needs separate checks.

fields.question: Does OmniKVQuant compress weights or the current context's KV cache?
fields.answer: It targets key/value states stored during inference, not fixed network parameters. Cache grows with context and contains different modality representations; quantized weights do not remove it.
fields.example: The same model has identical weights for short text and long audiovisual context, but different KV storage.

fields.question: How does modality-specific rotation differ from using one matrix for all values?
fields.answer: A shared rotation assumes one coordinate transform suits all modalities. Separate rotations allow distinct coordinate systems for audio, vision, and text. Accuracy still depends on calibration and actual distributions.
fields.example: Image and audio values may have different high-variance directions; one rotation might suit only one.

fields.question: Does the local 2-bit NumPy reference demonstrate a faster GPU KV kernel?
fields.answer: No. It checks window quantization and modality-specific transforms. Actual Triton or other kernels need real A100/A30 validation. Packing, unpacking, memory traffic, and fusion affect latency beyond bit width.
fields.example: Theoretically two-bit values stored and decoded in floating arrays do not yet deliver real two-bit VRAM or bandwidth savings.

fields.question: Why separate image scaling and question-dependent token extraction in PACE?
fields.answer: Scaling controls input encoding cost; extraction controls what continues downstream. Late token dropping cannot reclaim prior encoding. A shallow preview estimates difficulty, and extraction mixes language and visual attention by confidence rather than using one fixed rule.
fields.example: Shrink a blank image more than a dense menu, then use the question to select relevant regions.

fields.question: Why can't PACE infer equal vision budgets from equal image sizes?
fields.answer: Equal-sized images can differ in global semantic density and local detail. APC estimates both off-diagonal feature similarities and top-K details that differ from background. Pixel count is not a substitute, and budget signals do not guarantee correctness.
fields.example: A blank wall and a densely printed page at the same resolution need not preserve the same amount of detail.

fields.question: How does DDAE differ from an equal-weight attention average?
fields.answer: It converts the dispersions of two normalized attention maps into confidence weights using temperature softmax. Weights can favor different streams depending on evidence. Dispersion is a method signal, not a calibrated probability of correctness.
fields.example: Concentrated language attention and diffuse vision attention may favor language; another question can reverse the weights.
